chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 141 to 150, Ammuvanar's neythal decade on the njaazhal of the sand dune: every poem opens on the dune's njaazhal tree (its scent, clusters, birds, tide and waves) and turns to the shore lord, through pallor, sleeplessness and wasting to his return, the bride price and the friend's warning not to leave.

141.reading: The heroine says that the shore, where the njaazhal of the dune and the cherunthi spread their scent and the cold spray is flung in drops under the falling dew, has given her the pallor of longing.
141.nuance: She blames the place, not the man: the scented, cold, wet shore is made the agent (செய்தன) of her pallor, so the lover is accused only through his landscape.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred: the speaker suffers the pallor the shore has caused

142.reading: The heroine tells her friend she will not think of the lord of the shore, where birds settle on the low branch of the dune's njaazhal with its drooping clusters, so that her eyes may sleep.
142.nuance: The resolve is an admission: she must decide not to think of him precisely because thinking keeps her awake. The birds coming to roost on his shore while she cannot rest could be read as an implied contrast, but they do nothing a person of the situation does beyond resting, and the poem's sense does not need them, so they stay scene.

thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; the vocative தோழி and her own eyes (என் கண்ணே) fix the speaker

143.reading: The friend says that on the wide shore where birds cry by the dune's njaazhal, this girl's broad soft shoulders, which once gave delight, have afterwards come to give weariness.
143.nuance: இனிய செய்த நின்று பின் முனிவு செய்த sets the same shoulders on both sides of his change: what pleased him once now wearies him, or (on the other reading) now wastes and pains her.

144.reading: The heroine says that for the lord of the shore, where a lone heron sleeps in the grove under the dune's njaazhal heavy with clusters, her dark gleaming beauty has now turned pale.
144.nuance: இனி (now) marks a turn: the beauty was his once, and the pallor dates his neglect.

iraicchi.act: the solitary heron sleeps at ease in the flowering grove
iraicchi.sense: on his shore even a bird alone can sleep, while she, alone because of him, loses her colour

145.reading: The friend says the lord of the shore, where the tide draws at the great branches of the small-leaved njaazhal on the dune, has now removed the pallor of the dark girl.
145.nuance: Pallor is the one sign the man alone can cure; இனியே says the cure came only now, which the friend reports as his return to marry. The tide that bends the great branch has a single correspondence at most, so it is not ullurai.

146.reading: The heroine says that to the lord of the shore, where the dune's njaazhal opens its ripened buds into fragrant clusters, her dark gleaming beauty is surely sweet.
146.nuance: The buds that ripen and open beside the beauty that pleases him make a single match of mood, so it stays scene; மன்ற (surely) makes the claim a confident one.

147.reading: The friend says the lord of the shore, where women make bright leaf skirts with the flowers of the dune's njaazhal, has given his country as the price of the cool leaf skirt.
147.nuance: The leaf skirt, the small courting gift of the shore, is answered with a whole country: the friend's hyperbole turns the gift of secret love into a bride price. மலரின் could also be read as a simile (women like flowers), but the instrumental sense fits அயரும்.

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi

148.reading: The friend tells the heroine: embrace sweetly, you who love, the lord of the shore where the far-reaching great branch of the dune's njaazhal gives off its sweet-scented flowers.
148.nuance: இனிது is used twice, once of the flowers' scent and once of the embrace, so the shore's sweetness passes over into the union the friend now permits.

149.reading: The friend tells the man not to become one able to go away after he has nursed affliction in the young girl whose growing breasts bear spots like the flowers of the dune's njaazhal.
149.nuance: அகறல் வல்லாதீமோ blames a capacity rather than an act: do not be the kind of man who can leave. The affliction (அணங்கு) is something he has grown (வளர்த்து) in her, as her breasts are growing (வளர்).

150.reading: The heroine says the lord of the shore, where the sea waves sport about the great branch of the dune's njaazhal with its fragrant flowers, is bitter in union, a man hard to unite with.
150.nuance: The poem puns on புணரி (the wave) and புணர்வு (union): the sea's constant embrace stands against his rare one, and his union is bitter because it is rare.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 142's heroine resolves not to think of the shore lord so that her eyes may sleep; in Kural 1207 the woman says she does not know how to forget and asks what would become of her if she did.
links.teaches: The Sangam heroine treats not-thinking as a cure she can choose for her sleeplessness, while Valluvar's woman declares forgetting impossible and fatal, so the couplet denies exactly the resolve the older poem lets her voice.

links.note: Both close on the same line, உள்ளேன் தோழி படீஇயர் என் கண்ணே, after a bird-loud shore; Kuruntokai 243 fills the shore with girls playing at sand houses, Ainkurunuru 142 with birds settling to roost.
links.teaches: The refusal to think of him was a stock closing formula, and each poet earns it with a different shore picture, the girls' play recalling her past in one and the roosting birds setting her sleeplessness against their rest in the other.

links.note: The two poems end on the same words, என் மாமைக் கவினே, for the same shore lord: in 144 the beauty has turned pale, in 146 it is surely sweet to him.
links.teaches: Read together, the decade measures the whole state of the love by one phrase about her complexion, which can stand for neglect or for delight with nothing changed but the verb.

links.note: In Kural 1188 people say only that she has grown pale and never that he has left; in Ainkurunuru 145 the friend says the shore lord has now taken her pallor away.
links.teaches: The friend names the man as the one who can remove the pallor, which makes him its cause, so the Sangam poem supplies the very attribution that the couplet's woman complains no one makes.

links.note: In Natrinai 359 the hill lord's gift of a leaf skirt is a danger, since wearing it will alarm the mother; in Ainkurunuru 147 the shore lord gives his country as the price of the leaf skirt.
links.teaches: Held together, the two poems show the leaf skirt moving from a secret courting gift that cannot be worn openly to the token for which a bride price is paid, so the same object marks both ends of secret love.

links.note: Both are spoken to the man about to leave, by the friend on one reading of the Kural: Ainkurunuru 149 asks him not to become able to go after causing her affliction, Kural 1151 tells him to promise a quick return only to those who will survive it.
links.teaches: The Sangam friend still appeals to the man's character, asking him not to be the kind who can leave, whereas the couplet has given up persuasion and answers his promise with the threat of her death.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 150's heroine calls the shore lord bitter in union (புணர்வின் இன்னான்) and hard to unite with; in Kural 1152 the woman says union now holds pain for fear of parting.
links.teaches: Valluvar gives the reason the Sangam poem leaves implicit, that union turns bitter because parting is foreseen, while the poem's pun of the ever-embracing wave (புணரி) shows what that bitterness is measured against.

source_issues: 141-150: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade, so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem.
